section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: Prescott's portrayal of Cortés most clearly reflects

stimulus.text:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following excerpt.

The historian portrays Cortés as a daring and resourceful commander whose small Spanish force toppled the Aztec Empire through bold leadership, shrewd alliances with peoples subject to the Aztecs, and superior weaponry — while also recording the cruelty of the conquest.
—After William H. Prescott, History of the Conquest of Mexico, 1843 (paraphrased)

options: A. Abolitionist ideology and moral opposition to slavery
B. Nineteenth-century romantic admiration for heroic conquerors
C. Jacksonian democratic thought and egalitarian politics
D. Progressive muckraking journalism exposing corruption
items.explanation: Prescott's Cortés — daring, resourceful, toppling an empire with a handful of men — is the Romantic era's hero: the great man whose will shapes history. Writing in 1843, Prescott shared his age's admiration for heroic conquerors, even as he recorded the conquest's cruelty. The portrait is admiration first, moral accounting second — the nineteenth century's romantic way of writing about empire-builders.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Abolitionist ideology opposed slavery; Prescott's subject is a conquistador, not an abolitionist cause.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Prescott's portrayal reflects nineteenth-century romantic admiration for heroic conquerors.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Jacksonian egalitarianism celebrated the common man, not the heroic conqueror.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Progressive muckraking exposed corruption; Prescott wrote admiring narrative history.

items.stem: In the 1540s, Spanish critics of forced indigenous labor — including the Dominican friar Bartolome de Las Casas — helped bring about which of the following changes?

stimulus.image_caption: Theodor de Bry engraving illustrating Las Casas's account of Spanish cruelty, 1598.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Theodor de Bry, 1598, illustrating Bartolome de Las Casas; Smithsonian American Art Museum, CC0

options: (A) New royal limits on the encomienda and a growing reliance on enslaved African labor.
(B) A royal decree abolishing slavery throughout the entire Spanish Empire.
(C) Spain's abandonment of silver mining in favor of subsistence farming in its colonies.
(D) The drawing of a formal boundary separating indigenous lands from Spanish settlement zones.
items.explanation: Bartolomé de Las Casas's crusade against the enslavement and abuse of Native peoples helped produce the New Laws of 1542, which limited the encomienda system. But Spanish colonists needed labor, so the practical effect was a growing reliance on enslaved African labor to replace dying Native workers. Reform for Indians meant, tragically, expanded African slavery.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Las Casas's agitation brought new royal limits on the encomienda and a growing reliance on enslaved African labor.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. No royal decree abolished slavery throughout the Spanish Empire in the 1540s.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Spain did not abandon silver mining; it remained the empire's economic heart.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. No formal boundary separated indigenous lands from Spanish settlements as a result.

items.stem: Hakluyt's lament that England had never 'set fast footing' in America was driven chiefly by which of the following?

stimulus.text: "I marvel not a little . . . that since the first discovery of America (which is now full four score and ten years), after so great conquests and plantings of the Spaniards and Portuguese there, that we of England could never have the grace to set fast footing in such fertile and temperate places as are left as yet unpossessed of them. . . . I conceive great hope that the time approacheth . . . that we of England may share and part stakes (if we will ourselves) both with the Spaniard and the Portuguese in part of America . . ." — Richard Hakluyt, Divers Voyages Touching the Discovery of America, 1582

options: (A) Opposition to the power of the English monarchy.
(B) Concern for the welfare of Native American peoples.
(C) A desire to carry Protestantism to the peoples of Asia.
(D) Envy of Spanish and Portuguese colonial wealth and fear that England would be left behind.
items.explanation: Hakluyt marvels that after ninety years of Spanish and Portuguese conquests and plantings, England had still not set fast footing in America — and his tone is envy and anxiety. Spain's colonial wealth made England look poor and backward; Hakluyt feared England would be left behind in the race for empire. His lament is the voice of a nation coveting its rivals' riches.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Hakluyt served the monarchy's imperial ambitions; he did not oppose its power.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Concern for Native welfare was not Hakluyt's motive; colonial wealth was.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Hakluyt's focus was America, not carrying Protestantism to Asia.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Hakluyt was driven by envy of Spanish and Portuguese colonial wealth and fear England would be left behind.

items.stem: The first important cash crop in the American colonies was The 1874 illustration above shows John Rolfe, who pioneered tobacco cultivation in Virginia.

stimulus.image_caption: John Rolfe, who pioneered tobacco cultivation in Virginia (illustration, 1874).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1874; pre-1930

options: (A) cotton
(B) corn
(C) tea
(D) tobacco
items.explanation: John Rolfe's tobacco — the crop he pioneered in Virginia in the 1610s — was the first important cash crop of the American colonies. Tobacco exports saved Jamestown from collapse and made the Chesapeake economy. Cotton, corn, and tea came later or served other roles; tobacco was the colonies' first great money crop.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Cotton's boom came in the nineteenth century, long after tobacco.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Corn was a subsistence crop, not the first cash crop.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Tea was imported, not grown as a colonial cash crop.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Tobacco was the first important cash crop in the American colonies.

items.stem: The Mayflower Compact foreshadows the U.S. Constitution in which of the following ways?
options: (A) It posits the source of government power in the people rather than in God.
(B) It ensures both the right to free speech and the separation of church and state.
(C) It limits the term of office for all government officials.
(D) It establishes three branches of government in order to create a system of checks and balances.
items.explanation: The Mayflower Compact's signers covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic — creating government by their own mutual agreement. That act posits the people, not God or king, as the source of political authority: government by consent of the governed. The Constitution's We the People is the Compact's direct heir.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The Compact foreshadows the Constitution by positing the source of government power in the people.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Compact does not address free speech or church-state separation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Compact sets no term limits for officials.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Compact does not establish three branches or checks and balances.

items.stem: Which of the following most directly reflects de Bry's perspective in the image?

stimulus.image_caption: Theodor de Bry, 'The Natives of Florida Worship the Column Erected by the Commander on His First Voyage,' Grand Voyages, 1591 (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Theodor de Bry after Jacques Le Moyne, 1591; Library of Congress, pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: Questions 5-8 refer to the image above (replacing the bracketed description).

options: (A) {'letter': 'A', 'text': 'The natives of Florida are primitive and superstitious.'}
(B) {'letter': 'B', 'text': 'The natives of Florida are deeply Christian.'}
(C) {'letter': 'C', 'text': 'Europeans are unjustly exploiting the natives.'}
(D) {'letter': 'D', 'text': 'Conflict between natives and Europeans is inevitable.'}
items.explanation: Theodor de Bry's engravings of Florida — based on others' accounts, since he never crossed the Atlantic — depict Native peoples through a European lens of superiority: strange rituals, idol worship, customs presented as primitive curiosities. His images taught European readers to see the New World's peoples as primitive and superstitious, in need of European civilization. The perspective is condescension, not respect.

option_explanations.A: Correct. De Bry's perspective presents the natives of Florida as primitive and superstitious.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. De Bry does not depict the natives as Christian; he depicts them as heathen.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. De Bry's engravings do not condemn European exploitation; they reflect European superiority.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. De Bry does not argue conflict is inevitable; his theme is native primitiveness.

items.stem: Penn's Charter of Privileges is best seen as a forerunner of which of the following?

stimulus.text:
Questions 45–48 refer to the following document.

William Penn's Charter of Privileges, granted to the inhabitants of Pennsylvania and the Territories on October 28, 1701, which guaranteed religious toleration and representative government.

options: (A) {'letter': 'A', 'text': 'The Declaration of Independence'}
(B) {'letter': 'B', 'text': 'The Fourteen Points'}
(C) {'letter': 'C', 'text': 'The Gettysburg Address'}
(D) {'letter': 'D', 'text': 'The First Amendment to the Constitution'}
items.explanation: William Penn's Charter of Privileges (1701) guaranteed Pennsylvania's inhabitants religious toleration and representative government — rights held against authority. Those guarantees are the direct ancestors of the First Amendment's protections of religious liberty. Penn's charter was colonial America's great statement that conscience lies beyond the government's reach, and the Bill of Rights nationalized the principle.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Declaration proclaimed independence; Penn's charter concerned rights within government.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Fourteen Points were Wilson's World War I peace program.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Gettysburg Address concerned the Civil War's meaning, not religious toleration.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Penn's Charter of Privileges foreshadows the First Amendment's religious liberty.

items.stem: The most immediate consequence of the Proclamation of 1763 for British colonists was which of the following?

stimulus.text: "And We do further declare it to be Our Royal Will and Pleasure... to reserve under our Sovereignty, Protection, and Dominion, for the use of the said Indians... all the Lands and Territories lying to the Westward of the Sources of the Rivers which fall into the Sea from the West and North West... And We do hereby strictly forbid, on Pain of our Displeasure, all our loving Subjects from making any Purchases or Settlements whatever... of the Lands above reserved, without our especial leave and Licence for that Purpose first obtained." — Royal Proclamation of 1763

options: (A) A royal grant of western lands to French settlers as compensation for their wartime losses.
(B) A mass return migration of colonists to Britain in search of affordable farmland.
(C) The complete end of all trade between British colonists and American Indian nations.
(D) Resentment among land-hungry colonists and speculators who believed their wartime sacrifices had earned them access to western lands.
items.explanation: The Proclamation of 1763 forbade colonial settlement west of the Appalachians, reserving the territory for Native peoples. For colonists who had fought the French and Indian War expecting western lands as their reward — especially land-hungry settlers and speculators — the proclamation was a betrayal. Its most immediate consequence was their furious resentment at being denied the fruits of victory.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The proclamation did not grant western lands to French settlers.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Colonists did not return to Britain; they resented being kept from the West.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Trade with Native nations continued; settlement, not trade, was forbidden.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The proclamation's most immediate consequence was resentment among land-hungry colonists and speculators.

items.stem: Which reflects how many Americans responded to Jefferson's embargo?

stimulus.image_caption: 'Ograbme, or the American Snapping-Turtle,' embargo cartoon, 1807.
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: Questions 1-4 refer to the cartoon above (replacing the bracketed description).

options: A. Engaging in smuggling and illicit trade
B. Emigrating to other countries
C. Demanding war against France
D. Moving to the western frontier
items.explanation: Jefferson's Embargo Act of 1807 outlawed American trade with Britain and France, devastating port cities and ruining merchants. Many Americans responded not with obedience but with evasion: smuggling and illicit trade flourished along the Canadian border and the coast. The embargo made lawbreakers of ordinary traders.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Many Americans responded to the embargo with smuggling and illicit trade.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Mass emigration was not the response; evasion of the law was.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Americans did not demand war against France over the embargo.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Moving to the frontier was not the characteristic response; smuggling was.

items.stem: Cuffe's petition rests most directly on which Revolutionary-era principle?

stimulus.text: "We being chiefly of the African extract, and by reason of long bondage and hard slavery, we have been deprived of enjoying the profits of our labor.... yet... we have been, and now are, taxed both in our polls and that small pittance of estate which, through much hard labor and industry, we have got together.... while we are not allowed the privilege of freemen of the State, having no vote or influence in the election of those that tax us, yet many of our colour... have cheerfully entered the field of battle in the defence of the common cause, and that (as we conceive) against a similar exertion of power (in regard to taxation)." — Petition of Paul Cuffe and others, Dartmouth, Massachusetts, 1780

options: (A) The divine right of kings.
(B) The social contract as a justification for monarchy.
(C) No taxation without representation.
(D) Mercantilist regulation of colonial trade.
items.explanation: Paul Cuffe — a free Black mariner — and his fellow petitioners argued that Massachusetts taxed them while denying them the vote, the precise grievance the Revolution had been fought over. Having fought against taxation without representation, they demanded the principle apply to them: no taxation without representation. Their petition turns the Revolution's own logic against its exclusions.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Divine right of kings was the doctrine the Revolution rejected, not Cuffe's principle.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The social contract justifying monarchy was not Cuffe's argument.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Cuffe's petition rests on the Revolutionary principle of no taxation without representation.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Mercantilist trade regulation was not the petition's subject.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding a cause of the conflict referenced in the cartoon above?

stimulus.image_caption: 'The savages let loose, or The cruel fate of the Loyalists,' British cartoon, 1783 (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1783; Library of Congress British Cartoon Prints Collection, pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: The cartoon above: 'The savages let loose, or The cruel fate of the Loyalists' (1783).

options: (A) Britain’s defeat after the Seven Years’ War led to massive debt for the Crown, prompting an effort to collect taxes from the Thirteen Colonies.
(B) Emboldened by their victories during the Seven Years’ War, colonial elites challenged the Crown, pushing for independence before the working-class populace was ready to accept it.
(C) Britain’s massive debt after the Seven Years’ War resulted in a push for greater control over the Thirteen Colonies, sparking debate among colonists over the pursuit of independence.
(D) Disillusioned by their experiences in the Seven Years’ War, colonial militia members formed the Sons of Liberty, a radical group calling for independence from the Crown.
items.explanation: Britain emerged from the Seven Years' War victorious but buried in debt, and it moved to make the colonies pay: tighter enforcement, new taxes, greater imperial control. That push for control is what sparked colonial debate over whether independence was necessary. The war's debt caused the imperial crackdown that caused the revolutionary crisis.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Britain won the Seven Years' War; it was not defeated.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Colonial elites did not push for independence before the populace was ready; the debate followed Britain's control measures.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Britain's postwar debt drove its push for greater control, sparking colonial debate over independence.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Sons of Liberty formed later, in response to the Stamp Act, not from Seven Years' War militia experience.

items.stem: The weakness of the national government under the Articles of Confederation was shown by its inability to
options: A. Settle disputes between states
B. Raise an army
C. Conduct foreign relations
D. Print money
items.explanation: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could declare war but could not compel states to provide troops or money — it had to requisition both and hope. Shays's Rebellion exposed the emptiness: the national government could not raise an army to suppress a domestic uprising. The inability to raise an army was the Confederation's defining military weakness.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Congress could mediate state disputes; its weakness was enforcement power.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Articles government could not raise an army, as Shays's Rebellion proved.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Congress did conduct foreign relations, however weakly.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Congress could and did print money — continental currency.

items.stem: The Connecticut Plan at the Constitutional Convention proposed
options: A. A two-house legislature with both houses proportional to population
B. A single-house legislature based on proportional representation
C. A two-house legislature, one house proportional and one equal per state
D. A separation of powers among three branches
items.explanation: The Connecticut Compromise — the Connecticut Plan — broke the Convention's deadlock by creating a two-house legislature: the House apportioned by population (satisfying large states) and the Senate with equal representation per state (satisfying small states). Proportionality and equality each got a house. The Great Compromise shaped the Congress we still have.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Both houses proportional was the Virginia Plan, not the Connecticut compromise.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. A single proportional house was never the Connecticut proposal.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Connecticut Plan proposed a two-house legislature, one proportional and one equal per state.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Separation of powers was a separate principle, not the Connecticut Plan's content.

items.stem: Franklin's hostility to public poor relief most directly contrasts with which later development?

stimulus.text:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"I am for doing good to the poor, but ... I think the best way of doing good to the poor, is not making them easy in poverty, but leading or driving them out of it."
—Benjamin Franklin, 1766 (abridged)

options: A. The Monroe Doctrine
B. The spoils system
C. The New Deal's federal welfare programs
D. The protective tariff
items.explanation: Franklin's hostility to public poor relief — his insistence that making poverty comfortable only deepens it — stands in direct contrast to the New Deal's federal welfare programs. The New Deal built a national system of relief, Social Security, and aid to the poor on the opposite premise: that government should ease poverty's hardships. Franklin's philosophy and the welfare state are mirror opposites.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Monroe Doctrine concerned foreign policy, not poor relief.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The spoils system concerned patronage appointments, not welfare.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Franklin's hostility to poor relief contrasts most directly with the New Deal's federal welfare programs.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The protective tariff was an economic policy, not a welfare philosophy.

items.stem: Which of the following “miseries” alluded to above were most condemned by Anti-Federalists of the Post-Revolutionary Era?
options: (A) Organized response to Bacon’s Rebellion
(B) Federal response to Shays’s Rebellion
(C) Federal response to the Whiskey Rebellion
(D) Federal response to Pontiac’s Rebellion
items.explanation: The Anti-Federalists — the heirs of the Revolution's suspicion of centralized power — condemned Washington's 1794 military suppression of the Whiskey Rebellion as exactly the federal tyranny they had feared. Sending an army against Pennsylvania farmers proved, to them, that the new government would crush dissent. The federal response to the Whiskey Rebellion was their Exhibit A.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Bacon's Rebellion was 1676, a century before the Anti-Federalists.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Shays's Rebellion was suppressed by Massachusetts, not the federal government.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Anti-Federalists most condemned the federal response to the Whiskey Rebellion.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Pontiac's Rebellion was 1763, before the Anti-Federalists existed.

items.stem: In the late 1800s, federal policy toward Native Americans shifted from that shown above to
options: (A) a recognition of equal Native American sovereignty
(B) attempts to assimilate Native Americans through individual land grants
(C) establishment of land reservations for Indigenous tribes
(D) granting of American citizenship to Native groups
items.explanation: In the late 1800s, federal Indian policy shifted from the earlier pattern of removal and reservation confinement to assimilation: the Dawes Act of 1887 broke reservations into individual land allotments, aiming to turn Native peoples into private-property farmers and dissolve tribal life. The goal was no longer separation but absorption — making Indians into individual landowners on the American model.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The shift was not toward recognizing equal sovereignty; it was toward assimilation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Federal policy shifted to attempts to assimilate Native Americans through individual land grants.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Reservations were the earlier policy being dismantled, not the new direction.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Military conquest was not the late-1800s shift; allotment and assimilation were.

items.stem: Jackson's 'Bank War' is most comparable as a policy to

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1836 (lithograph by Henry R. Robinson; Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the cartoon described below.

The 1836 cartoon 'General Jackson Slaying the Many Headed Monster' shows President Andrew Jackson, dressed as a soldier, raising a cane to strike a many-headed serpent. Each head wears a crown labeled with the name of a Bank director or ally, and the creature is labeled 'Bank of the United States.'

options: A. Clay's 'American System'
B. McKinley's 'Full Dinner Pail'
C. Theodore Roosevelt's 'trust-busting'
D. Johnson's 'Great Society'
items.explanation: Jackson's Bank War — his veto of the recharter and destruction of the Second Bank of the United States — was a presidential assault on concentrated corporate power. Its closest parallel is Theodore Roosevelt's trust-busting: another president using executive power to break up great combinations he saw as threats to the republic. Both were populist attacks on monopoly power from the White House.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Clay's American System promoted a national bank; Jackson destroyed one.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. McKinley's Full Dinner Pail celebrated protective prosperity, not war on concentrated power.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Jackson's Bank War is most comparable to Theodore Roosevelt's trust-busting — presidential assaults on concentrated economic power.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Johnson's Great Society was a domestic welfare program, not an attack on a great corporation.

items.stem: Although the Supreme Court was the weakest of the three branches of government in the early days of the new republic, John Marshall strengthened the Court by
options: (A) establishing the principle of federalism, giving federal courts the power to declare laws unconstitutional
(B) declaring the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, which asserted the right of states to nullify federal laws, unconstitutional
(C) establishing the principle of judicial review in the case of McCulloch v. Maryland
(D) establishing the principle of judicial review in the case of Marbury v. Madison
items.explanation: John Marshall took a Court that Jeffersonians dismissed as the weakest branch and made it the Constitution's authoritative interpreter. Through Marbury v. Madison (judicial review), McCulloch v. Maryland (implied powers), and Gibbons v. Ogden (commerce power), he established the federal judiciary's supremacy over constitutional questions. Marshall's Court gave the new republic its legal backbone.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Federalism's balance was debated, but Marshall's great achievement was judicial review, not inventing federalism.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Marshall never declared the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions unconstitutional; they faded politically without a Court ruling.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. McCulloch v. Maryland established implied powers and federal supremacy, but judicial review was established in Marbury.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Marshall strengthened the Court by establishing judicial review in Marbury v. Madison.

items.stem: As a result of the Mexican–American War, all of the following became part of the United States EXCEPT

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1848 by E. Gilman. Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) California
(B) Nevada
(C) New Mexico
(D) Texas
items.explanation: The Mexican-American War ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848), by which Mexico ceded California, Nevada, New Mexico, and the rest of the Mexican Cession to the United States. Texas was not part of that cession: it had been annexed in 1845, before the war began — indeed, the dispute over Texas helped cause the war. Texas was already American; the war's prize was the Far West.

option_explanations.A: This did become part of the U.S. as a result of the war, so it is not the answer. California was ceded in 1848.
option_explanations.B: This did become part of the U.S. as a result of the war, so it is not the answer. Nevada was part of the Mexican Cession.
option_explanations.C: This did become part of the U.S. as a result of the war, so it is not the answer. New Mexico was ceded in 1848.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Texas was annexed in 1845, before the Mexican-American War; it was not a result of the war.

items.stem: The sentiment expressed in the cartoon above is continuous with criticisms of all of the following federal policies from the 1900s EXCEPT

stimulus.text: King Andrew the First , Unknown Artist, c. 1833

options: (A) Franklin Roosevelt’s proposals for Supreme Court reform
(B) Richard Nixon’s use of presidential power to cover up the Watergate break-in
(C) Ronald Reagan’s funding of anti-communist forces in Nicaragua
(D) Bill Clinton’s reform of welfare laws
items.explanation: The King Andrew the First cartoon attacks Jackson for executive tyranny — a president trampling constitutional limits. That same criticism echoed through the twentieth century against FDR's court-packing scheme, Nixon's Watergate abuses, and Reagan's Iran-Contra defiance of Congress. Bill Clinton's welfare reform does not belong: it was ordinary legislation passed by Congress, not an executive power grab. The cartoon's theme is presidential overreach, and welfare reform wasn't one.

option_explanations.A: This criticism is continuous, so it is not the answer. FDR's court-packing was attacked as executive overreach.
option_explanations.B: This criticism is continuous, so it is not the answer. Nixon's Watergate cover-up was the classic abuse of presidential power.
option_explanations.C: This criticism is continuous, so it is not the answer. Reagan's Contra funding defied Congress like Jackson defied his critics.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Clinton's welfare reform was legislation, not executive overreach.

items.stem: Jackson attacked the Second Bank of the United States because he believed

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1836 (lithograph by Henry R. Robinson; Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the cartoon described below.

The 1836 cartoon 'General Jackson Slaying the Many Headed Monster' shows President Andrew Jackson, dressed as a soldier, raising a cane to strike a many-headed serpent. Each head wears a crown labeled with the name of a Bank director or ally, and the creature is labeled 'Bank of the United States.'

options: A. It was an undemocratic financial monopoly
B. It meddled in the slavery debate
C. It gave the president too much financial power
D. It refused to fund internal improvements
items.explanation: Andrew Jackson attacked the Second Bank of the United States as a monster: a private corporation, controlled by wealthy stockholders and foreign investors, wielding vast financial power without answering to the people. To Jackson it was an undemocratic financial monopoly — concentrated economic power corrupting the republic. The Bank War was democracy's war on monopoly.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Jackson attacked the Bank as an undemocratic financial monopoly.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Bank did not meddle in the slavery debate; Jackson's objection was to its concentrated power.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Jackson feared the Bank's power over the economy, not that it gave the president too much financial power.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Internal-improvement funding was not Jackson's grievance against the Bank.

items.stem: Dix's method — investigating conditions firsthand and petitioning legislatures — most closely resembles the tactics of

stimulus.text:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following excerpt.

"I come to present the strong claims of suffering humanity. I come as the advocate of helpless, forgotten, insane, and idiotic men and women... I proceed, gentlemen, briefly to call your attention to the present state of insane persons confined within this Commonwealth, in cages, closets, cellars, stalls, pens! Chained, naked, beaten with rods, and lashed into obedience."
—Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts, 1843 (abridged)

options: A. Antebellum reformers like temperance and abolitionist activists
B. Southern planters defending the institution of slavery
C. Jacksonian office-seekers pursuing patronage positions
D. Manifest Destiny expansionists promoting western settlement
items.explanation: Dorothea Dix investigated asylum conditions firsthand, documented the horrors, and petitioned legislatures for reform — the classic method of antebellum reformers. Temperance crusaders and abolitionists worked the same way: expose the evil, arouse public conscience, demand legislative action. Dix's moral investigation belongs to the great age of American reform movements.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Dix's investigate-and-petition method matches antebellum reformers like temperance and abolitionist activists.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Southern planters defended slavery; they did not investigate and petition against abuses.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Jacksonian office-seekers pursued patronage, not moral reform through investigation.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Expansionists promoted settlement; they did not petition legislatures about asylum conditions.

items.stem: Black Codes were instituted to
options: A. To expand Black political participation
B. To strengthen the Freedmen's Bureau
C. To bar Black workers from many occupations
D. To preserve slavery in the Deep South
items.explanation: The Black Codes were Southern laws designed to control freedpeople's labor: vagrancy statutes, occupational restrictions, and apprenticeship laws that barred Black workers from many occupations and forced them into plantation labor. Their purpose was economic — to keep Black Southerners as a dependent workforce, restoring the substance of slavery under new legal forms.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Codes restricted Black rights; they did not expand political participation.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Codes undermined the Freedmen's Bureau's work, not strengthened it.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Black Codes were instituted to bar Black workers from many occupations and control their labor.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Slavery itself was dead; the Codes recreated its economic substance without the name.

items.stem: Lincoln's pledge to leave slavery 'alone where it is' was meant to

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photographed February 27, 1860 by Mathew Brady (Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; PD tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following quotation.

"Wrong as we think slavery is, we can yet afford to leave it alone where it is … but can we, while our votes will prevent it, allow it to spread into the National Territories, and to overrun us here in these Free States? … LET US HAVE FAITH THAT RIGHT MAKES MIGHT, AND IN THAT FAITH, LET US, TO THE END, DARE TO DO OUR DUTY AS WE UNDERSTAND IT." —Abraham Lincoln, Cooper Union Address, February 27, 1860 (abridged)

options: A. Promise the immediate abolition of slavery
B. Reassure the South he would not interfere with slavery where it existed
C. Endorse the Dred Scott decision
D. Call for Southern secession
items.explanation: Lincoln's pledge to leave slavery alone where it existed was aimed at Southern fears: he needed the South to believe a Republican president would not touch slavery in the states. The promise was reassurance — accept my election, and your institution is safe where the Constitution protects it. Lincoln offered containment of slavery's spread, not interference with its existence.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Lincoln promised the opposite of immediate abolition in 1860.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The pledge was meant to reassure the South he would not interfere with slavery where it existed.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Lincoln did not endorse Dred Scott; he attacked the decision.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Lincoln opposed secession; he did not call for it.

items.stem: The sentiments above are most consistent with which of the following ideologies?

stimulus.text: “On the 4th day of March next, this party will take possession of the Government. It has announced that…a war must be waged against slavery until it shall cease throughout the United States. “The guaranties of the Constitution will then no longer exist; the equal rights of the States will be lost. The slave-holding States will no longer have the power of self-government, or self-protection, and the Federal Government will have become their enemy. “Sectional interest and animosity will deepen the irritation, and all hope of remedy is rendered vain, by the fact that public opinion at the North has invested a great political error with the sanction of more erroneous religious belief. We, therefore, the People of South Carolina…have solemnly declared that the Union heretofore existing between this State and the other States of North America, is dissolved, and that the State of South Carolina has resumed her position among the nations of the world, as a separate and independent State.” Source: “Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union,” 1860

options: (A) States’ rights
(B) Nullification
(C) Neutrality
(D) Civil disobedience
items.explanation: South Carolina's 1860 secession declaration argues that the federal government has become the enemy of the slaveholding states, that equal rights of the states are lost, and that the state resumes its independent position. That is the ideology of states' rights: the Union as a compact of sovereign states, each free to judge federal overreach and withdraw. Secession was states' rights carried to its ultimate conclusion.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The secession sentiments express the ideology of states' rights.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Nullification was the 1830s tariff doctrine; secession went beyond nullifying a law to leaving the Union.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Neutrality concerned foreign wars, not the sectional crisis.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Civil disobedience was Thoreau's individual protest, not a state's secession theory.

items.stem: Which of the following best expresses Thomas Nast's perspective in the cartoon?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published October 24, 1874 (Harper's Weekly; Thomas Nast). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A political cartoon by Thomas Nast, 'The Union as It Was / The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery,' Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874: members of the White League and the Ku Klux Klan shake hands across a skull, while a Black family cowes in terror beneath them.]

options: (A) {'letter': 'A', 'text': 'The Reconstruction of the South is succeeding.'}
(B) {'letter': 'B', 'text': 'The government is failing to protect freed Black people.'}
(C) {'letter': 'C', 'text': 'White Southerners must stand together.'}
(D) {'letter': 'D', 'text': 'Reconstructing Southern society was a mistake.'}
items.explanation: Thomas Nast's Reconstruction cartoons showed the federal government standing by while white terrorist groups murdered freedpeople — his message was that Washington was failing to protect Black Southerners. Nast, a Radical Republican sympathizer, indicted the government's weakness: the laws existed, but the will to enforce them against the Klan and White Leagues did not. His cartoons demanded federal protection for freedpeople.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Nast showed Reconstruction failing, not succeeding.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Nast's perspective was that the government was failing to protect freed Black people.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Nast attacked white Southern terrorism; he did not call for white solidarity.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Nast supported Reconstruction; he did not call it a mistake.

items.stem: Bruce's emphasis on patience and self-improvement differed most sharply from

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I have confidence, not only in this country and her institutions, but in the endurance, capacity, and destiny of my people. We will, as opportunities arise, continue to prove ourselves worthy of the responsibilities that citizenship imposes."
—Senator Blanche K. Bruce (R-MS), speech in the U.S. Senate, 1870s (abridged)

options: A. W. E. B. Du Bois's demand for immediate civil rights and higher education
B. Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Compromise
C. Southern sharecroppers' desire for land of their own
D. Abraham Lincoln's emancipation policy
items.explanation: Blanche Bruce — the Black Mississippi senator — preached patience, self-improvement, and confidence in American institutions. That gradualism differed most sharply from W. E. B. Du Bois, who demanded immediate civil rights and higher education for Black Americans, denouncing patience as surrender. Bruce counseled endurance; Du Bois demanded justice now.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Bruce's patience differed most sharply from Du Bois's demand for immediate civil rights and higher education.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Compromise also preached patience and self-improvement — similar to Bruce, not sharply different.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Sharecroppers' desire for land was economic, not the philosophical contrast the question seeks.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Lincoln's emancipation policy was wartime necessity, not a gradualist philosophy.

items.stem: The Cooper Union Address helped Lincoln by

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photographed February 27, 1860 by Mathew Brady (Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; PD tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following quotation.

"Wrong as we think slavery is, we can yet afford to leave it alone where it is … but can we, while our votes will prevent it, allow it to spread into the National Territories, and to overrun us here in these Free States? … LET US HAVE FAITH THAT RIGHT MAKES MIGHT, AND IN THAT FAITH, LET US, TO THE END, DARE TO DO OUR DUTY AS WE UNDERSTAND IT." —Abraham Lincoln, Cooper Union Address, February 27, 1860 (abridged)

options: A. Making him a Union general
B. Electing him to the Senate in 1858
C. Introducing him to eastern Republicans ahead of the 1860 nomination
D. Ending the Civil War
items.explanation: Lincoln was a little-known Illinois lawyer when he spoke at New York's Cooper Union in February 1860. The address — a brilliant constitutional argument against slavery's expansion — introduced him to eastern Republicans, the men who would decide the nomination. Cooper Union made Lincoln a national figure and a credible presidential contender.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Lincoln never became a Union general; he was commander in chief as president.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Lincoln lost the 1858 Senate race to Douglas; Cooper Union came afterward.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Cooper Union Address introduced Lincoln to eastern Republicans ahead of the 1860 nomination.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The address was 1860; the war ended in 1865.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement set by the Reconstruction Act of 1867 for southern states’ readmission to the Union?
options: (A) Black people had to be allowed to participate in state conventions and state elections.
(B) The state had to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution.
(C) The state had to pay reparations and provide land grants to all former enslaved people.
(D) The state had to rewrite its constitution and ratify it.
items.explanation: The Reconstruction Act of 1867 required Southern states to let Black men vote in conventions and elections, ratify the Fourteenth Amendment, and write new constitutions — the price of readmission. It did not require reparations or land grants to former slaves; no such provision existed. Land redistribution was debated but never made a condition of readmission.

option_explanations.A: This was a requirement, so it is not the answer. Black participation was mandated.
option_explanations.B: This was a requirement, so it is not the answer. Ratifying the Fourteenth Amendment was required.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the NOT. Reparations and land grants were never a readmission requirement.
option_explanations.D: This was a requirement, so it is not the answer. New constitutions had to be written and ratified.

items.stem: The conditions Nast depicts contributed most directly to which of the following?

stimulus.text:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A political cartoon by Thomas Nast, 'The Union as It Was / The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery,' Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874: members of the White League and the Ku Klux Klan shake hands across a skull, while a Black family cowes in terror beneath them.]

options: (A) {'letter': 'A', 'text': 'The Fifteenth Amendment'}
(B) {'letter': 'B', 'text': 'The Homestead Act offering settlers free land'}
(C) {'letter': 'C', 'text': 'The New South industrialization movement'}
(D) {'letter': 'D', 'text': "The Supreme Court's Plessy v. Ferguson decision"}
items.explanation: Nast's 1874 cartoon — the White League and Klan shaking hands over a skull while a Black family cowers — depicted the terrorist violence engulfing Reconstruction's final years. Those conditions contributed most directly to the Supreme Court's retreat from Reconstruction's promises, culminating in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which blessed segregation. The violence Nast showed helped kill the political will that Plessy then buried legally.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) preceded the cartoon; the conditions led away from its promise.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Homestead Act concerned western settlement, not Southern racial terror.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. New South industrialization was an economic movement, not the cartoon's consequence.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The conditions Nast depicts contributed to the climate that produced Plessy v. Ferguson.

items.stem: Americans joined the political process in this era for all of the following reasons EXCEPT
options: A. Campaign parades and rallies excited the public
B. The evenly matched parties produced close races
C. Spreading newspapers informed more voters
D. The era's presidential candidates were dynamic figures
items.explanation: Gilded Age Americans voted in astonishing numbers — often 80 percent of eligible voters — drawn by campaign parades and rallies, by evenly matched parties producing cliffhanger races, and by a spreading newspaper press that informed more voters. The era's presidential candidates, however, were famously not dynamic figures; they were often colorless party regulars chosen for availability, not charisma. High turnout came from party loyalty and spectacle, not magnetic candidates.

option_explanations.A: This did draw Americans in, so it is not the answer. Parades and rallies excited the public.
option_explanations.B: This did draw Americans in, so it is not the answer. Close races between evenly matched parties energized voters.
option_explanations.C: This did draw Americans in, so it is not the answer. Spreading newspapers informed more voters.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The era's presidential candidates were generally undynamic party regulars, not magnetic figures.

items.stem: The “free silver” campaign of 1896 received its greatest popular support from

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1896 cartoon by F. Opper (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons; LOC print.
stimulus.text_stimulus: “We have witnessed for more than a quarter of a century the struggles of the two great political parties for power and plunder, while grievous wrongs have been inflicted upon the suffering people. We charge that the controlling influences dominating both these parties have permitted the existing dreadful conditions to develop without serious effort to prevent or restrain them. Neither do they now promise us any substantial reform. They have agreed together to ignore, in the coming campaign, every issue but one. They propose to drown the outcries of a plundered people with the uproar of a sham battle over the tariff, so that capitalists, corporations, national banks, rings, trusts, watered stock, the demonetization of silver and the oppressions of the usurers may all be lost sight of. They propose to sacrifice our homes, lives, and children on the altar of mammon; to destroy the multitude in order to secure corruption funds from the millionaires. “Assembled on the anniversary of the birthday of the nation, and filled with the spirit of the grand general and chief who established our independence, we seek to restore the government of the Republic to the hands of ‘the plain people,’ with which class it originated. We assert our purposes to be identical with the purposes of the National Constitution; to form a more perfect union and establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the common defence, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty for ourselves and our posterity.” Source: Populist Party Platform, 1892

options: (A) New England businessmen, who were discriminated against under the existing banking system
(B) southern women, who incorporated it into a larger campaign for economic equality
(C) bankers, who had run out of paper currency to invest
(D) farmers, who hoped that a more generous money supply would ease their debt burdens
items.explanation: The free-silver campaign of 1896 — William Jennings Bryan's crusade for the free coinage of silver — drew its greatest popular support from farmers. Debt-burdened by mortgages and falling crop prices, farmers hoped a more generous money supply would raise prices and ease their debts. Free silver was the farmers' monetary salvation: more dollars, lighter debts.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. New England businessmen favored the gold standard; they opposed free silver.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Southern women were not the core of free-silver support; indebted farmers were.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Bankers favored sound money and the gold standard, not free silver.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Farmers gave free silver its greatest support, hoping inflation would ease their debt burdens.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about Supreme Court decisions during the latter part of the 19th century is most accurate?
options: (A) They reduced federal power over the states by narrowly defining the applicability of the Constitution to state law.
(B) They cleared the way for the liberal reforms of the 20th century by broadly interpreting constitutional guarantees of individual rights.
(C) They had little practical effect because the executive branch consistently refused to enforce the Court’s rulings.
(D) They used the Fourteenth Amendment to create numerous environmental regulations and human rights, stifling American business growth.
items.explanation: In the late nineteenth century, the Supreme Court — in cases like the Civil Rights Cases (1883) and Plessy (1896) — narrowly defined the Constitution's protections, reducing federal power over the states and gutting Reconstruction's guarantees. The Court read the Fourteenth Amendment as a thin shield, leaving states free to segregate and discriminate. The era's decisions contracted federal authority, not expanded it.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Late-1800s decisions reduced federal power over the states by narrowly reading the Constitution's application to state law.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Court did not clear the way for liberal reforms; it blocked them with narrow readings.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The executive generally enforced or acquiesced in these rulings; non-enforcement was not the pattern.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Court did not create environmental regulations or broad human rights; it narrowed rights.

items.stem: Urban political machines endured because they provided

stimulus.pd_rationale: Harper's Weekly, 1871-10-21 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A Thomas Nast cartoon depicting Tammany Hall boss William M. Tweed as a bloated, grasping figure looming over New York City.]

options: A. Honest, efficient government
B. Opposition to federal power
C. Help and services for the poor
D. Rights unavailable outside the city
items.explanation: Urban political machines endured because they provided what the poor needed: jobs, food, coal, bail money, help with landlords — tangible services in exchange for votes. The machine was the immigrant's welfare office before government welfare existed. Help and services for the poor were the machine's currency and its foundation.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Machines were notoriously corrupt, not honest and efficient.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Machines worked within the system; opposing federal power was not their purpose.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Machines endured because they provided help and services for the poor.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Machines did not grant special rights; they traded services for votes.

items.stem: Carnegie's outlook, as criticized in the cartoon, drew on which idea?
options: (A) The Social Gospel
(B) 'Survival of the fittest'
(C) The Gospel of Wealth
(D) 'Rugged individualism'
items.explanation: Carnegie's outlook — the one the cartoon criticizes — was his Gospel of Wealth: the doctrine that the rich are merely stewards of their fortunes, duty-bound to give them away for libraries, universities, and public goods. The cartoon's charge is that this philosophy was funded by crushing workers; the giving was noble in theory, but the getting was ruthless. Carnegie's gospel justified great wealth by its charitable use.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Social Gospel demanded Christians reform society to help the poor; Carnegie's doctrine justified the rich giving from above.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Survival of the fittest was Sumner's Social Darwinism, a different justification of wealth.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Carnegie's outlook drew on the Gospel of Wealth — the rich as stewards duty-bound to give.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Rugged individualism celebrated self-reliance generally; Carnegie's specific doctrine was the Gospel of Wealth.

items.stem: Which other charge was commonly leveled against Carnegie?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1892 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Wikimedia Commons file page.

options: (A) That as an immigrant he had no legitimate right to own controlling interests in major American industries
(B) That he tolerated violence against workers who demanded better conditions
(C) That his reputation as America's richest man was undeserved
(D) That his charity favored Scotland over the United States
items.explanation: Beyond the philanthropy funded by exploitation, Carnegie faced the charge that he tolerated violence against workers who demanded better conditions — most infamously at Homestead in 1892, when his manager Henry Clay Frick called in Pinkerton detectives who battled striking steelworkers. Men died so the union could be broken. The charge was that Carnegie's profits rested on crushed labor.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Carnegie's immigrant origins were not the charge; his labor practices were.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Carnegie was charged with tolerating violence against workers demanding better conditions — Homestead above all.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. No one disputed that Carnegie was America's richest man; the dispute was how he treated workers.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Carnegie's charity favored American libraries and institutions; Scotland was not the issue.

items.stem: Defenders of the corporate practices Rice describes would most likely have appealed to which of the following?
options: (A) Herbert Spencer's Social Darwinism, which cast great wealth as fitness.
(B) Henry George's proposal for a single tax on land values.
(C) The Populist Omaha Platform's demands for government intervention.
(D) Upton Sinclair's The Jungle and its expose of the meatpacking industry.
items.explanation: Defenders of Gilded Age corporate practices — the trusts, the wage cuts, the union-busting — appealed to Herbert Spencer's Social Darwinism: the idea that economic competition was nature's law, the wealthy were the fit, and the poor deserved their fate. Spencer gave ruthlessness a philosophy. What Rice's corporate defenders needed was a moral theory of inequality, and Social Darwinism supplied it.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Corporate defenders appealed to Spencer's Social Darwinism, which cast great wealth as fitness.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Henry George's single tax attacked concentrated wealth; defenders would never invoke it.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Omaha Platform demanded government curb corporations — the opposite of a defense.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Sinclair's Jungle attacked industry; it was a weapon against corporations, not for them.

items.stem: The 1933 political cartoon shown above makes the point that

stimulus.text: [Described image — 1933 political cartoon titled ‘Strike-Breaking’ (original artwork not reproduced). Two burly thugs, one labeled ‘STRIKE-BREAKING’ and the other ‘UNION-BUSTING,’ beat a helpless worker with clubs. In the foreground, a small figure labeled ‘FACT-FINDING’ — a government investigator — crawls on all fours holding a magnifying glass, deliberately looking away from the violence. The cartoon charges that employers violently repressed unions while the federal government offered only a willfully blind, ineffectual ‘fact-finding’ response.]

options: (A) infighting within and among unions prevented their rise to economic power
(B) government inspectors turned their backs to illegal repression of labor unions
(C) attacks on unions were so well-concealed that the government did not know where to begin its investigations
(D) from their beginnings, labor unions were controlled by organized crime
items.explanation: The 1933 Strike-Breaking cartoon shows employer thugs beating a worker while the government fact-finder crawls past with a magnifying glass, deliberately looking away. Its point is that government inspectors turned their backs on the illegal repression of labor unions — offering willfully blind investigations instead of protection. The cartoon indicts the state's complicity through inaction.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The cartoon shows employer violence and government blindness, not union infighting.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The cartoon's point is that government inspectors turned their backs to the illegal repression of labor unions.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The attacks were open, not concealed; the cartoon shows the government seeing and ignoring them.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The cartoon does not claim unions were controlled by organized crime.

items.stem: The cartoon's ideas most directly reflect which continuity in American history?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photograph by Lewis Hine, c. 1911 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.

options: (A) Ongoing debates over the proper role of government in regulating the economy.
(B) Ongoing debates over the proper role of political parties.
(C) Ongoing debates over states' power to defy federal authority.
(D) Ongoing debates over whether communities may outlaw behavior they deem immoral.
items.explanation: The cartoon's ideas — about government power over business, regulation, and the economy — belong to the long American debate over the proper role of government in regulating the economy. From the Bank War through the New Deal to modern regulation, Americans have argued endlessly about how much the state should restrain or direct economic life. The cartoon is one voice in that permanent argument.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The cartoon reflects ongoing debates over government's proper role in regulating the economy.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The role of political parties is not the cartoon's subject.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. States defying federal authority is not the continuity at issue.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Outlawing immoral behavior is a different debate from economic regulation.

items.stem: Which of the following most strongly tried to block or undo the changes Cohen describes?
options: (A) Communist Party radicals and other political radicals.
(B) Organizations lobbying for senior citizens.
(C) Civil-rights groups such as the Congress of Racial Equality.
(D) Conservatives in Congress and on the Supreme Court.
items.explanation: Lizabeth Cohen describes industrial workers' journey toward the welfare state and union acceptance — the New Deal transformation. The forces that most strongly tried to block or undo those changes were conservatives in Congress and on the Supreme Court: Southern Democrats and Republicans who fought labor law, and justices who struck down New Deal measures. Reaction came from the right, in both branches.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Communists and radicals supported the changes; they did not block them.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Senior-citizen lobbies were not the chief opponents of New Deal labor changes.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Civil-rights groups like CORE allied with labor's advance, not against it.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Conservatives in Congress and on the Supreme Court most strongly tried to block or undo the changes.

items.stem: Which earlier federal action most closely resembled the Meat Inspection Act's approach?

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1900 photograph (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons; LOC print.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"For the purposes hereinbefore set forth the Secretary shall cause to be made, by inspectors appointed for that purpose, an examination and inspection of all cattle, sheep, swine, and goats before they shall be allowed to enter into any slaughtering, packing, or canning establishment..."
—Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906 (abridged)

options: A. The creation of the Interstate Commerce Commission (1887) to regulate railroads
B. The Homestead Act's distribution of western land
C. The Chinese Exclusion Act's ban on immigration
D. The Sherman Antitrust Act's dissolution of Standard Oil
items.explanation: The Meat Inspection Act (1906) put federal inspectors inside packing plants — the government's eyes on private industry. The earlier federal action that most closely resembled that approach was the creation of the Interstate Commerce Commission (1887), which put federal regulators over the railroads. Both marked the same development: Washington directly supervising private business in the public interest.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The ICC's railroad regulation most closely resembled the Meat Inspection Act's approach — direct federal supervision of industry.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Homestead Act distributed land; it did not regulate industry.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Chinese Exclusion restricted immigration; it did not supervise business practices.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Sherman Act broke up trusts through courts; inspection was continuous administrative supervision.

items.stem: Coolidge's argument would be weakest against which criticism?

stimulus.text:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)

options: A. That the income tax is unconstitutional
B. That Britain levied higher taxes
C. That farmers opposed protective tariffs
D. That an industrial nation needs public goods only government can provide
items.explanation: Coolidge argued that heavy taxation destroys the right to enjoy the rewards of one's industry. That argument would be weakest against the criticism that an industrial nation needs public goods only government can provide — roads, schools, courts, defense — which must be paid for somehow. If taxation funds necessities no private actor will supply, then the right to untaxed rewards cannot be absolute.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The income tax's constitutionality was settled by the Sixteenth Amendment; this is not the weak point.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Britain's higher taxes do not answer whether Americans need taxed public goods.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Farmers' views on tariffs are beside the point of Coolidge's taxation argument.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Coolidge's argument is weakest against the need for tax-funded public goods only government can provide.
