items.stem: Lodge's reference to the 'mongrel banner invented for a league' expresses his

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"You may call me selfish if you will, conservative or reactionary, or use any other harsh adjective you see fit to apply, but an American I was born, an American I have remained all my life. I can never be anything else."
—Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, 1919 (abridged)

options: A. his support for unrestricted immigration
B. his admiration for the League's flag
C. his contempt for divided international allegiance
D. his indifference to national symbols
items.explanation: Lodge's sneer at the mongrel banner invented for a league expresses his contempt for divided international allegiance — the idea that Americans might owe loyalty to a League flag alongside the Stars and Stripes. To Lodge, the League demanded Americans split their patriotism, and he would have none of it. An American I was born, an American I have remained: one flag, one loyalty.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Lodge was a restrictionist, not a supporter of unrestricted immigration.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Lodge despised the League's banner; he did not admire it.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The phrase expresses Lodge's contempt for divided international allegiance.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Lodge cared intensely about national symbols; he was not indifferent to them.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about organized labor in the early 1900s is true?
options: (A) Throughout the early 1900s, Congress promoted the interests of labor unions over captains of industry.
(B) Immigrants helped to promote a more diverse workforce less reliant on child labor.
(C) Sharecroppers in the South largely voted for Democrats who championed labor causes.
(D) unions such as the American Federation of Labor bargained directly with employers for workplace changes
items.explanation: In the early 1900s, unions like the American Federation of Labor — organized by craft, led by Samuel Gompers — bargained directly with employers for concrete workplace changes: higher wages, shorter hours, safer conditions. Business unionism, not revolution, was the AFL's method. The true statement is the modest one: unions negotiated directly with bosses for bread-and-butter gains.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Congress generally favored industry over unions in this era; courts issued anti-union injunctions.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Immigrants did diversify the workforce, but child labor remained widespread.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Southern sharecroppers were largely disenfranchised and did not vote for labor champions.
option_explanations.D: Correct. AFL unions bargained directly with employers for workplace changes.

items.stem: Republicans called Democrats 'soft on communism' for all of the following EXCEPT
options: A. China went Communist under Truman
B. Alger Hiss had advised FDR at Yalta
C. Truman set up no loyalty-check system
D. Wartime deals eased the Soviet takeover of Eastern Europe
items.explanation: Republicans called Democrats soft on communism by citing China's fall under Truman, Alger Hiss's role advising FDR at Yalta, and wartime deals that eased the Soviet takeover of Eastern Europe. What they could not cite was Truman's failure to set up a loyalty-check system — because he did set one up: Executive Order 9835 (1947) created the federal employee loyalty program. The charge collapses on the one claim that isn't true.

option_explanations.A: Republicans did cite this, so it is not the answer. China's 1949 fall was blamed on Truman.
option_explanations.B: Republicans did cite this, so it is not the answer. Hiss at Yalta was a staple charge.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Truman did set up a loyalty-check system (Executive Order 9835).
option_explanations.D: Republicans did cite this, so it is not the answer. The Yalta deals were attacked as selling out Eastern Europe.

items.stem: Which of the following best represents an effect of the legal decision described above?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USArmy}}: U.S. Army photograph. Public domain.
stimulus.text_stimulus: “We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’ has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. Therefore, we hold that the plaintiffs and others similarly situated for whom the actions have been brought are, by reason of the segregation complained of, deprived of the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment.” Source: Brown v. Board of Education , 1954

options: (A) Continuing white resistance slowed efforts at desegregation, sparking a series of social conflicts throughout the South.
(B) The Supreme Court decision from Brown v. Board of Education led to increased enrollment in colleges and universities.
(C) During the 1960s, increasing numbers of high school graduates rejected the notion that a college education was desirable.
(D) In the 20th century, jobs in advanced technical and medical industries generally require postgraduate degrees.
items.explanation: The legal decision described is Brown v. Board of Education (1954), and its effect was massive white resistance: Southern states closed public schools, opened segregation academies, and defied court orders, sparking social conflicts from Little Rock to Oxford. Desegregation did not proceed smoothly; continuing white resistance slowed it and produced a decade of Southern crises.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Brown's effect was continuing white resistance that slowed desegregation and sparked Southern conflicts.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Brown did not directly drive college enrollment increases; its effect was the desegregation struggle.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. High school graduates did not reject college in the 1960s; enrollment grew.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Postgraduate job requirements are a different trend, not Brown's effect.

items.stem: The ideas in the cartoon most directly reflect which continuity in twentieth-century American history?
options: (A) Continuing debates over the proper role of political parties.
(B) Continuing debates over political means and ends.
(C) Continuing debates over executive versus legislative power.
(D) Continuing debates over federal regulation of the economy.
items.explanation: The cartoon's ideas — about how political ends justify or condemn political means — reflect the continuing twentieth-century debate over political means and ends. From the Palmer Raids to Watergate to the war on terror, Americans have argued over whether noble goals excuse ignoble methods. The cartoon is one entry in that permanent argument about how far power may go.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The role of parties is not the cartoon's subject.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The cartoon reflects continuing debates over political means and ends.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Executive-versus-legislative power is a different debate.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Federal economic regulation is not the cartoon's theme.

items.stem: All of the following were part of Johnson’s Great Society program EXCEPT

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov-POTUS}}: official White House photograph, a work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.
stimulus.text_stimulus: “The challenge of the next half century is whether we have the wisdom to use wealth to enrich and elevate our national life, and to advance the quality of our American civilization…. The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all. It demands an end to poverty and racial injustice, to which we are totally committed in our time. But that is just the beginning. The Great Society is a place where every child can find knowledge to enrich his mind and to enlarge his talents. It is a place where leisure is a welcome chance to build and reflect, not a feared cause of boredom and restlessness. It is a place where the city of man serves not only the needs of the body and the demands of commerce but the desire for beauty and the hunger for community. It is a place where man can renew contact with nature. It is a place which honors creation for its own sake and for what it adds to the understanding of the race. It is a place where men are more concerned with the quality of their goals than the quantity of their goods. But most of all, the Great Society is not a safe harbor, a resting place, a final objective, a finished work. It is a challenge constantly renewed, beckoning us toward a destiny where the meaning of our lives matches the marvelous products of our labor.” Source: Lyndon Johnson, Remarks at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, 1964

options: (A) the Civil Rights Act of 1964
(B) Medicare and Medicaid
(C) the establishment of the Department of Housing and Urban Development
(D) the balanced budget mandate
items.explanation: Johnson's Great Society included the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Medicare and Medicaid, and the new Department of Housing and Urban Development — a vast expansion of federal social policy. A balanced budget mandate was never part of it; Great Society liberalism accepted deficits as the price of reform. Fiscal restraint was the opposite of the program's spirit.

option_explanations.A: This was part of the Great Society, so it is not the answer.
option_explanations.B: This was part of the Great Society, so it is not the answer. Medicare and Medicaid were 1965 landmarks.
option_explanations.C: This was part of the Great Society, so it is not the answer. HUD was created in 1965.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. No balanced budget mandate was part of Johnson's Great Society.

items.stem: Feminist highlights of the era included all of the following EXCEPT
options: A. The founding of Ms. magazine
B. The formation of NOW
C. Ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment
D. Greater awareness of women's issues
items.explanation: The feminist movement of the era founded Ms. magazine (1972), formed the National Organization for Women (1966), and raised national awareness of women's issues. The Equal Rights Amendment was not ratified — it fell three states short in 1982 despite the campaign. The ERA's defeat, not its triumph, is the era's story.

option_explanations.A: This was a feminist highlight, so it is not the answer. Ms. magazine was founded in 1972.
option_explanations.B: This was a feminist highlight, so it is not the answer. NOW was formed in 1966.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The Equal Rights Amendment was never ratified.
option_explanations.D: This was a feminist highlight, so it is not the answer. Awareness of women's issues grew enormously.

items.stem: The 'creed' whose 'true meaning' King invokes — 'that all men are created equal' — comes from

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USNWR}}: U.S. News & World Report photograph held by the Library of Congress with no known copyright restrictions. Public domain.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 25–28 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

King told the marchers not to 'wallow in the valley of despair,' declaring his dream that America would one day live out the true meaning of its creed — that all men are created equal.
—After Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., 'I Have a Dream,' 1963

options: A. The Gettysburg Address
B. The Declaration of Independence's equality principle
C. The Constitution's preamble
D. The Emancipation Proclamation
items.explanation: When King declared I have a dream rooted in the American dream that all men are created equal, the creed he invoked comes from the Declaration of Independence's equality principle. Jefferson's words — all men are created equal — were the moral foundation King claimed for the civil rights movement. The true meaning of the creed was the Declaration's promise, unfulfilled and now demanded.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Gettysburg Address echoed the creed, but its source is the Declaration.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The creed comes from the Declaration of Independence's equality principle.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Constitution's preamble begins We the People; the equality creed is Jefferson's.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Emancipation Proclamation freed slaves; it did not originate the equality creed.

items.stem: The excerpt above can best be used as evidence to prove which of the following historical claims?

stimulus.text: “We found that not only was it a civil war, an effort by a people who had for years been seeking their liberation from any colonial influence whatsoever, but also we found that the Vietnamese whom we had enthusiastically molded after our own image were hard put to take up the fight against the threat we were supposedly saving them from. “We found most people didn’t even know the difference between communism and democracy. They only wanted to work in rice paddies without helicopters strafing them and bombs with napalm burning their villages and tearing their country apart. They wanted everything to do with the war, particularly with this foreign presence of the United States of America, to leave them alone in peace, and they practiced the art of survival by siding with whichever military force was present at a particular time, be it Viet Cong, North Vietnamese or American.” Source: Statement by John Kerry of Vietnam Veterans Against the War

options: (A) By the 1970s, antiwar sentiment had moved beyond a fringe position
(B) Soldiers were more likely to oppose the Vietnam War than civilians.
(C) Prolonged spending on the Vietnam conflict was creating domestic economic challenges.
(D) Republicans owed their electoral success to their Vietnam position.
items.explanation: John Kerry's 1971 testimony — describing Vietnam as a civil war, Vietnamese villagers wanting only to be left alone, and American power as the destructive foreign presence — can best prove that by the 1970s, antiwar sentiment had moved beyond a fringe position. A decorated veteran testifying before Congress showed opposition had entered the mainstream. The excerpt is evidence of antiwar feeling's breadth, not just its existence.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The excerpt proves antiwar sentiment had moved beyond a fringe position by the 1970s.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The excerpt does not compare soldiers' and civilians' opposition rates.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Domestic economic effects of war spending are not the excerpt's subject.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Republican electoral success is not what the testimony demonstrates.

items.stem: Coolidge's warning against heavy taxation most directly continued the tradition of

stimulus.text:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)

options: A. Hamiltonian support for a national bank
B. Jeffersonian opposition to energetic federal government
C. Jacksonian enthusiasm for internal improvements
D. Whig support for the American System
items.explanation: Coolidge's 1924 warning against heavy taxation — that it destroys the right to enjoy industry's rewards — continued the Jeffersonian tradition of opposing energetic federal government. Jeffersonians feared concentrated federal power and championed limited government, low taxes, and individual liberty. Coolidge's economy crusade was Jefferson's small-government creed in twentieth-century dress.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Hamilton championed energetic federal government, including a national bank — Coolidge's opposite.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Coolidge continued the Jeffersonian tradition of opposing energetic federal government.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Jacksonians favored internal improvements; Coolidge favored economy and restraint.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Whigs supported the American System's active government; Coolidge opposed it.

items.stem: During the 1990s, President George H. W. Bush

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov}}: work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.

options: (A) signed the welfare reform bill
(B) persuaded Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin to sign the Camp David Accords
(C) sent troops to fight in the Persian Gulf War
(D) cut taxes and social services
items.explanation: During the 1990s, President George H. W. Bush sent American troops to fight in the Persian Gulf War (1991), expelling Iraq from Kuwait in Operation Desert Storm. The welfare reform bill was Clinton's, Camp David was Carter's, and cutting taxes and services was Reagan's. The Gulf War was Bush's defining presidential act.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Clinton signed welfare reform in 1996, not Bush.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Camp David Accords were Carter's 1978 achievement.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Bush sent troops to fight in the Persian Gulf War.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Cutting taxes and services was Reagan's program, not Bush's.

items.stem: Reagan's warning against 'simpleminded appeasement' most directly recalls the American lesson drawn from

stimulus.text:
Questions 5–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

President Reagan urged Americans to pray for those living under totalitarian rule — but until they found freedom, he warned, the West must stay vigilant and strong against the Soviet threat.
—After President Ronald Reagan's 'evil empire' speech, 1983

options: A. The Munich Agreement with Nazi Germany
B. The Treaty of Versailles
C. The League of Nations' peacekeeping record
D. The Kellogg-Briand Pact
items.explanation: Reagan's 1983 warning against simpleminded appeasement of the Soviets recalled the American lesson of the Munich Agreement: that appeasing Nazi Germany in 1938 only invited greater aggression. Munich taught Americans that dictators exploit weakness and that peace requires strength. Reagan's anti-appeasement stance was Munich's lesson applied to the Cold War.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Reagan's warning recalls the lesson of the Munich Agreement with Nazi Germany.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Versailles was about punishing Germany after World War I, not about appeasement.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The League's peacekeeping record was a different lesson about collective security.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Kellogg-Briand Pact outlawed war generally; Munich was the specific appeasement lesson.

section_1b.directions: Section I, Part B — Short Answer: 3 questions, 40 minutes. Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (A, B, C); write your answers in complete sentences. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, Question 2 on a primary source, and Question 3 on a non-text source (map, chart, image, or diagram). This part counts for 20 percent of the exam score.

questions.stimulus_text: Historian Lisa McGirr argues that the late twentieth century saw 'the triumph of a new conservatism' — as suburban activists, evangelical Christians, and free-market economists reshaped American politics from the grassroots up.
parts: A. Briefly explain ONE example of the conservative direction of the nation in the 1970s and 1980s.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND example of that conservative direction.
C. Briefly explain ONE Cold War approach taken by a 1970s or 1980s president.
exemplar: Nixon's 'law and order' campaign (1968) and 'Southern strategy' courted voters alienated by civil rights, urban riots, and antiwar protest.
Reagan's election (1980) sealed the turn: tax cuts, deregulation, and attacks on 'big government' embodied a new conservative governing creed.
Cold War approaches varied: Nixon and Kissinger pursued détente with Moscow and the opening to China, while Reagan confronted the 'evil empire' with an arms buildup.

questions.stimulus_text: For we must consider that we shall be as a city upon a hill. The eyes of all people are upon us.
questions.attribution: John Winthrop, 'A Model of Christian Charity,' sermon aboard the Arbella, 1630.
parts: A. Briefly describe Winthrop's warning to the Puritan colonists in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE reason Puritans migrated to New England in the 1630s.
C. Briefly explain ONE longer-term effect of Winthrop's 'city upon a hill' idea on American thought.
exemplar: Winthrop warns the Puritan colonists that their new community will be watched by the whole world as a model - their success or failure will prove whether a godly commonwealth can flourish.
The Puritans migrated to escape Archbishop Laud's persecution of nonconformists and the political turmoil of Charles I's England, seeking a place to practice their reformed faith.
Winthrop's 'city upon a hill' became a lasting American self-image: the idea that the United States has a special, exemplary mission in the world persisted long after Puritan New England.

questions.stimulus_text: The photograph shows a power house mechanic - an adult worker in overalls - straining to operate a massive steam pump in an industrial plant. The machinery dwarfs him; grease, heat, and physical danger are evident in the close, dark composition.
questions.attribution: Described from the 1920 photograph by Lewis Hine (Wikimedia Commons).
parts: A. Briefly describe what the photograph shows about industrial work in the early twentieth century.
B. Briefly explain ONE way reformers attempted to address the conditions shown in the photograph.
C. Briefly explain ONE way the Supreme Court limited Progressive labor reforms.
exemplar: The photograph shows an ordinary worker performing skilled, dangerous industrial labor - humanizing the factory workforce that Progressive reformers sought to protect.
Reformers responded with state and federal labor laws: workers' compensation statutes, limits on working hours, and the Keating-Owen Child Labor Act (1916) all aimed to curb industrial exploitation.
The Supreme Court limited these reforms in cases like Lochner v. New York (1905) and Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918), striking down labor laws as violations of liberty of contract or of federalism.

section_2a.directions: Section II, Part A — Document-Based Question: 1 question, 60 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period). The question is based on 7 documents. In your response you must develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, use at least 4 documents to support your argument, use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents, and for at least 2 documents explain how the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to your argument. This part counts for 25 percent of the exam score.

dbq.prompt: Americans debated and addressed immigration policy in the period 1754–1800 and again in the period 1875–1925. Evaluate the extent to which the ways they debated and addressed immigration changed between the two periods.

documents.text: Why should the [Germans] be suffered to swarm into our Settlements, and by herding together establish their Language and Manners to the Exclusion of ours? Why should Pennsylvania, founded by the English, become a Colony of Aliens, who will shortly be so numerous as to Germanize us instead of our Anglifying them, and will never adopt our Language or Customs, any more than they can acquire our Complexion.
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: Franklin writes as an English Pennsylvanian watching German immigrants 'swarm' into his colony. Purpose: to warn that unchecked German immigration will 'Germanize' Pennsylvania rather than Anglicize the newcomers. Audience: colonial readers of his pamphlet. Why it matters: the document shows nativist cultural anxiety predating the republic itself — the early period's debate was framed around cultural assimilation and colonial identity, not yet around federal legislation.

documents.text: What then is the American, this new man? He is either an European, or the descendant of an European, hence that strange mixture of blood, which you will find in no other country. I could point out to you a family whose grandfather was an Englishman, whose wife was Dutch, whose son married a French woman, and whose present four sons have now four wives of different nations. He is an American, who leaving behind him all his ancient prejudices and manners, receives new ones from the new mode of life he has embraced, the new government he obeys, and the new rank he holds. He becomes an American by being received in the broad lap of our great Alma Mater. Here individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men, whose labours and posterity will one day cause great changes in the world.
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: Crevecoeur, a French immigrant turned American farmer, writes as a celebrant of his adopted country. Purpose: to present America as a transformative 'melting pot' where Europeans shed old prejudices and become a new people. Audience: European readers of his widely read Letters. Why it matters: written partly to attract European interest, the document idealizes American openness — the optimistic counter-voice in the early period's debate, and the ancestor of the twentieth century's 'melting pot' language.

documents.text: And shall we alone adopt the rash theory that the subjects of all governments despotic, monarchical, and aristocratical are, as soon as they set foot on American ground, qualified to participate in administering the sovereignty of our country? Shall we hold the benefits of American citizenship so cheap as to invite, nay, almost bribe, the discontented, the ambitious, and the avaricious of every country to accept them? . . . A war, the most cruel and dreadful which has been known for centuries, was now raging in those in all those countries from which emigrants were to be expected. . . . Could any reasonable man believe, that men who, actuated by such passions, had fought on grounds so opposite, almost equally distant from the happy mean we had chosen, would here mingle in social affections with each other, or with us?
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: Sedgwick, a Federalist congressman, speaks amid the wars of the French Revolution, when French radicalism seemed contagious. Purpose: to persuade the House to restrict naturalization by portraying immigrants as carriers of Europe's violent passions. Audience: fellow congressmen debating the Naturalization Bill. Why it matters: the document shows the early period's debate turning on political loyalty and national security — whether newcomers from warring Europe could be trusted with republican citizenship.

documents.text: The cry that the 'Chinese must go' is both narrow and unjust. It represents no broad or universal principle. It is merely a repetition of the cry that was raised years ago by American Indians against the immigration of Irishmen, Englishmen, Germans and others from European nations. It now ill becomes those, or the descendants of those, against whom this cry was raised in past years, to raise a similar tocsin against a class of foreigners who have been degraded by ages of oppression. . . . The feeling at the bottom of the 'Know Nothing' movement IN ITS EARLY DAYS was certainly a general one against low wages, and if it had raised the cry: No low wages. No cheap labor! Instead of sounding the intolerant, silly, and shameful cry against Irishmen, Englishmen, Germans and all other 'foreigners,' it would have accomplished incalculable good.
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: McDonnell writes as a labor journalist defending Chinese immigrants. Purpose: to rebut the 'Chinese must go' cry as narrow and unjust, redirecting workers' anger from foreigners to the low-wage system — and to shame descendants of earlier immigrants for repeating Know-Nothing bigotry. Audience: working-class readers of the Labor Standard. Why it matters: the document is a class-based pro-immigration voice from inside the labor movement, showing the later period's debate was not simply workers versus immigrants.

documents.text: [Image description: Joseph Keppler's 1880 cartoon presents the United States as a great ark afloat on rough seas, taking immigrant families of many nations aboard while dark storm clouds mass over Europe behind them — America pictured as a haven from Old World turmoil, open to all.]
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: Keppler, himself an Austrian-born immigrant, draws from the immigrant's perspective. Purpose: to portray the United States as Noah's ark — a refuge carrying immigrants to safety while storm clouds gather over troubled Europe. Audience: the mass readership of Puck, America's leading humor magazine. Why it matters: the cartoon's optimism comes from an immigrant celebrating the welcome he received; it is the later period's visual counterpart to Crevecoeur's melting-pot ideal.

documents.text: These new immigrants were no longer exclusively members of the Nordic race as were the earlier ones who came of their own impulse to improve their social conditions. The transportation lines advertised America as a land flowing with milk and honey, and the European governments took the opportunity to unload upon careless, wealthy, and hospitable America the sweepings of their jails and asylums. The result was that the new immigration, while it still included many strong elements from the north of Europe, contained a large and increasing number of the weak, the broken, and the mentally crippled of all races drawn from the lowest stratum of the Mediterranean basin and the Balkans, together with hordes of the wretched, submerged populations of the Polish Ghettos.
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: Grant, a wealthy anthropologist and eugenicist, writes with the authority of early-twentieth-century racial 'science.' Purpose: to warn that 'new' immigrants from southern and eastern Europe are biologically inferior to the earlier 'Nordic' stock. Audience: educated elites and policymakers. Why it matters: the document shows how the later period's nativism dressed itself in pseudoscientific racism — a harder, more categorical exclusionism than the early period's cultural worries, and the intellectual fuel for the 1920s quota laws.

documents.text: [Image description: Frank Beard's 1885 cartoon shows the female figure of Columbia recoiling as a crowd of 'unwelcome guests' presses in on her; behind them, vermin stream from drains marked with the names of Italy, Russia, and Germany, while the arriving figures are tagged as anarchists, socialists, and members of the Mafia — a warning against unrestricted immigration.]
documents.sourcing_note: Historical situation: Beard drew this in 1885, amid a surge of southern and eastern European immigration and a wave of labor militancy (the Knights of Labor neared 800,000 members). Purpose: to persuade readers that unrestricted immigration endangers America by depicting newcomers as rats, anarchists, socialists, and Mafiosi pouring from the 'sewers' of Italy, Russia, and Germany. Audience: popular magazine readers. Why it matters: the cartoon fuses economic, criminal, and radical stereotypes into visual propaganda — the later period's nativism at its most visceral, aimed at mass persuasion rather than elite debate.

Develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, and support your argument with specific and relevant examples. This part counts for 15 percent of the exam score.
